title: Model-Guided Microstimulation Steers Primate Visual Behavior
one_liner: Train an artificial brain model to predict how a monkey sees, then use it to find the best spots to stimulate real monkey cortex to show them what you want them to see.
lead: Neuroscientists can zap monkey brain with tiny electrodes to trigger visual experiences, but old methods are clumsy: they only work for simple shapes like letters because they target the brain's low-level detail regions and run out of electrodes. This paper makes a leap: use a trained artificial brain model to figure out WHERE and HOW to stimulate the monkey's higher-level regions (where complex object recognition lives) so they perceive complex objects — faces, scenes, arbitrary images — with far fewer electrodes.

problem.h2: Brain stimulation is stuck in the shallow end
paras: Today's visual prosthetics (electronic implants meant to restore vision) do brain stimulation in the early visual cortex — the part that handles raw pixels and edges. It works for simple things: zap the right spot, the monkey sees a letter. But early cortex has room for only a few electrodes (because of space), and worse, it only represents simple features. A beginner tries the obvious: put electrodes where they pick up specific letters or shapes. This breaks at complexity: letters map to small regions; faces map to vast regions, scattered across higher cortex, and require patterns too intricate to program by hand.

High-level visual cortex (where the monkey recognizes complex objects) would be a better target because each neuron there is already tuned to a category (faces, scenes, objects), so you need fewer electrodes to evoke the same experience. But you cannot simply guess where to stimulate; the circuits are too intricate and the anatomy differs from monkey to monkey.

callout.html: Use a computer model of the monkey's brain to predict which spots to stimulate and how, then test those predictions in the real brain.

panels.title: 1. The old way: electrodes stuck in the shallow
panels.viz_args: Early cortex: V1, V2. Simple features (edges, lines). Limited by electrode count. Cannot do complex objects.
panels.caption: Old prosthetics target early cortex where electrodes fit. Encodes only simple shapes.

panels.title: 2. High-level cortex is the goal
panels.viz_args: Higher cortex: IT. Complex objects (faces, scenes). Richer detail. Fewer electrodes needed.
panels.caption: Higher cortex represents complex objects but stimulation targets there are unknown.

panels.title: 3. Train a model of the monkey's brain
panels.caption: Build an artificial neural network trained to predict what the monkey sees in response to images.

panels.title: 4. Use the model to find optimal stimulation
panels.caption: Simulate electrode placement in the model and test which sites best steer behavior.

panels.title: 5. Deploy to real monkey, measure success
panels.caption: Test model predictions in vivo. Real electrodes, real monkey, real behavioral choices.

steps.text: Build a deep learning model (topographic network) that mimics how real monkey cortex responds to images and learns to organize itself spatially, just like real neurons do.

steps.b: Step 2: Align model to the monkey's recorded activity
steps.text: Wire up both the model and the electrodes to watch the same 4,000 images, find which model neurons correspond to which implanted electrodes by matching their response patterns, so the model is now a digital copy of that specific monkey's brain layout. This alignment is critical because it lets you translate model predictions to real electrode coordinates.

steps.b: Step 3: Simulate stimulation in the model
steps.text: Ask the model: if I stimulated this spot, would the monkey behave as though it saw a face? Test thousands of candidate electrode sites and stimulation patterns in silico (in the computer).
Keep the electrode sites where the model predicts the strongest, most reliable visual experience — measured by how confidently the model says the monkey made the choice you intended.

steps.b: Step 5: Run the experiment in the real monkey
steps.text: Stimulate the top-ranked sites on the actual implanted electrodes, alternating between real pulses and sham (fake) pulses, while the monkey performs a visual recognition task. Measure whether the real behavior matches the model prediction.

object.h2: The object: stimulation site and pattern
paras: The paper does not change the monkey's brain or the stimulation hardware. It changes WHERE you stimulate (electrode site and timing within the grid) and WHAT stimulation pattern you use (which sequence of pulses). Instead of guessing these based on simple rules, the model searches a vast space of possibilities and proposes the best candidates.

hidden.name: how well model activity predicts monkey choice
paras: The core quantity the paper measures is how tightly the model's neural activity (at the candidate stimulation site, under the proposed stimulation) correlates with what the monkey actually does. In plain terms: if you tell the model to simulate a stimulation pulse that represents a face, does the model's high-level cortex light up in a way that says face? The better the match, the likelier the real monkey will see a face when you stimulate that spot, because the model learned to mimic how the real brain processes images and decisions.

The paper estimates this using a two-alternative-forced-choice (2AFC) task: the monkey sees two images and picks the one it prefers. The model predicts which image the monkey will choose by measuring how similar the top-layer representation is to each image. Stimulation that shifts the model's choice toward faces tells you which real electrodes to target.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger alignment between model activity and actual monkey choice. Highlighted sites are top candidates for real implantation.

reads.html: The paper finds sites where stimulation makes the model behave exactly as the monkey would, so those sites are safe bets for the real experiment.

The metric is the Pearson correlation between model-predicted 2AFC choices (under simulated stimulation) and the ground-truth monkey choices, ranked across candidate sites to select maximal behavioral steering.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: four reasons aligned
paras: Early cortex is hard to stimulate for complex tasks because there is too little space and the neurons encode too little detail. The model solves this by targeting higher cortex, which already separates and labels complex objects: faces in one spot, scenes in another. Stimulating high-level cortex directly shifts those object labels, so the monkey perceives the object you chose.

But where in high-level cortex? The model learns to organize itself spatially, the same way real brains do, by penalizing artificial neurons that are close together but respond differently to the same images (spatial smoothing loss). Because the model is spatially faithful, you can trust that if a spot in the model looks like it encodes faces, the corresponding spot in the real monkey's brain probably does too.

Why does simulation predict real behavior? Because the model was trained on the monkey's own neural recordings, carefully aligned to the monkey's brain coordinates. The model is not generic; it is a digital copy of that individual monkey's visual cortex. When you perturb the model, you are essentially asking: what would the monkey's own brain do in this scenario?

Finally, the mapping procedure translates model sites to real sites using shared reference images. Both the model and the monkey see the same 4,000 images, and the paper finds which model neurons fire like which real electrodes for those images. This alignment is the lock-and-key that transfers model predictions to the physical implant.

stages.s: Passive recordings: 4,000 images, monkey watches, electrodes listen
Train model on images to predict neuron activity, with spatial smoothing loss
Align model layer to implanted electrode array by matching response correlation
Simulate stimulation at each candidate site in the model, predict 2AFC choice
Rank sites by choice prediction confidence, select top candidates
Test on real monkey: does predicted site trigger the intended behavior?

math.h2: The spatial loss: enforce nearby neurons to agree
math.words: Total training loss is task loss plus 0.25 times the spatial-loss term in each layer. The spatial loss measures how well nearby artificial neurons have correlated responses compared to how close they are physically. If two neurons are far apart but respond alike, the loss increases. If they are close but respond differently, the loss increases. Only nearby neurons that respond alike keep the loss low, so the model learns to organize like real cortex.
math.equation: Loss_total = L_task + sum_k (0.25 * SL_k) where SL_k = 1 - Corr(r, D), and r is response-correlation between unit pairs, D is inverse-distance weighting (1 / distance + 1)
symbols: classification or prediction error on the images (main training goal)
layer index (different levels of the artificial brain)
weight on spatial loss (how much to care about spatial organization)
spatial loss in layer k (penalizes spatial disorder)
Pearson correlation between response-similarity pairs and distance-weighted pairs
Pearson correlation of responses between units i and j across images
inverse distance weight: 1 / (distance_ij + 1), nearby pairs get higher weight

worked.title: A tiny worked example with three artificial neurons
lines: Setup: neurons A, B, C are placed at (0,0), (1,0), (5,5) in 2D cortical space.
A and B are close (distance 1); B and C are far (distance ~7).
Response data: A and B have responses with Pearson correlation 0.9 (they agree). B and C have correlation 0.2 (they disagree).
The spatial loss compares Corr(r, D). If r = [0.9, 0.2] and D = [0.5, 0.125], their correlation is high (close pairs agree, far pairs disagree). The loss 1 - Corr(r, D) is small, training is happy.
If instead A and C had been close but disagreed (r = 0.2, D = 0.5), Corr(r, D) would be low and loss would be high, penalizing the disorder. Training nudges A and C to respond alike.

math.note: This loss teaches the artificial brain to organize itself spatially, so nearby artificial neurons behave alike and the model mirrors the real brain's layered geography.

bars.h2: Old method vs. guided method: behavior accuracy in simulation

charts.title: Naive method (random sites)
charts.note: Random stimulation confuses the monkey and contradicts the intended object.

charts.title: Model-guided method
charts.note: Model-optimized stimulation reliably tilts the monkey's perception toward the target, measured by choice prediction agreement.

items.html: If the model is trained on a different dataset or different monkey, its spatial organization may not match the target monkey's brain. Alignment to the target monkey's passive recordings is critical — skip this and predictions fail.

Real electrodes can shift position or lose sensitivity over hours. If the model was aligned on day 1 but stimulation happens on day 5, the model's predictions may not map to the actual electrode sites anymore.
Electrical pulses create large artifacts in the recordings that can swamp the neural signal. If the model was trained on clean passive data but tested under stimulation noise, the alignment breaks.

items.b: Shallow cortical targets may not encode the intended object.
items.html: If the chosen stimulation site in high-level cortex does not truly encode faces (e.g., it is a mixedregion responding to multiple object categories), stimulating it will evoke a confused percept, not a clear face.

Aligning the model to each monkey individually, stimulating within hours of recording, targeting deep high-level areas with verified selectivity, and quantifying confidence in predictions all push the method toward success.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo would train a topographic model on a public dataset (ImageNet or faces), align it to synthetic electrode data (either from another trained model or from a published dataset of real neural recordings), then optimize electrode sites and stimulation patterns to steer the model's two-alternative-forced-choice predictions. Finally, report how often the model's predicted choice matches a held-out set of ground-truth monkey choices. The key is to show that model-optimized sites achieve 75+ percent agreement with actual choices, versus 50 percent for random sites — a clear lift that proves the model's predictions transfer to real brains.
demo.metric_eq: Behavioral steering success = fraction of trials where stimulation-predicted choice matches actual monkey choice, compared to baseline random-site choice accuracy
demo.closing: The demo must prove that in-silico stimulation predicts in-vivo behavior, so a user can see that the model is not just abstract — it transfers to real decision-making.
